newsitem.title: CANADA: Union sees progress with GM Canada.
newsitem.headline: Union sees progress with GM Canada.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers Union President Buzz Hargrove told reporters on Monday that the union expects to win concessions on outsourcing from General Motors Corp's Canadian unit.
Hargrove said he had "good discussions" with GM Canada's lead negotiator, Dean Munger, which could end a dispute over the sale of two plants in Canada and the loss of 5,500 jobs.
Earlier, Hargrove had threatened to call off talks if sufficient progress was not made on the key issue of contracting out.
"It is enough for me to say to our bargaining committee that we can continue talking," Hargrove said.

He said the discussion was the first indication the company might reverse the plan to outsource at two major Ontario plants, the Oshawa fabrication plant and the Windsor trim plant. It could also affect an outsourcing plan at GM's axel plant in St. Catharines, Ontario.
"It's the first indication that they would do anything short of continuing with their business plan on sale, closure or wind down at the three plants that have been identified," Hargrove said.

GM Canada spokesman, Stew Low, told Reuters after the press conference that it might not reverse its decisions, but that both sides are developing some creative ideas to resolve the outsourcing issue.
"I think reverse is probably pretty strong," he said. (But) "I think there is some light at the end of the tunnel."
Union officials said Hargrove expected to meet with GM Canada lead negotiator, Dean Munger, later Monday night.
The union chose GM Canada one week ago as its second negotiating target after reaching agreement with Chrysler Canada earlier this month.

The Chrysler pact, ratified last weekend, halts plant sales and closings during the three-year agreement and commits Chrysler to replace any union jobs lost due to work done by outside contractors, known as outsourcing.

Hargove said the union has approved an escalating strike strategy that would close down GM operations in Oshawa and St. Therese, Quebec. He said members will walk out of GM's St. Catharines plant on October 6 and close down remaining plants in London and Windsor, Ontario, on October 9.
Neither the company nor the union would speculate on the cost of a strike.
But analysts said last week that a strike could cost GM as much as $150 million a week, halt production of some vehicle models and interrupt U.S. operations.

"A long strike might get to the point where it would be reducing GM's profits by maybe $100 million to $150 million a week," said Dave Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. "It could spread south of the (Canada/U.S.) border as well."
However, the United Auto Workers union, which reached a tentative agreement with Chrysler and has ratified a deal with Ford, must now turn to GM in the next couple of weeks.
